subtopics.title: Free Basic Water — The Policy and the Promise

questions.question: The free basic water policy entitles every poor household each month to:
options: 60 000 litres
6 000 litres — six kilolitres — of clean water free of charge
600 litres
25 litres

questions.question: The six kilolitre figure is calculated from:
options: The average size of a municipal dam
The monthly rainfall of Johannesburg
25 litres per person per day for a household of eight
150 litres per person per day for a family of four

questions.question: The rising block tariff is double-edged because it:
options: Charges everyone the same rate per litre
Applies only to farms
Makes all water free in drought years
Protects the poor in the cheap first blocks while charging heavy users rates that discourage waste

questions.question: Access on paper is not water in the hand means:
options: A household counted as having access may share a distant standpipe or depend on broken infrastructure
The constitution does not mention water
Households must apply in writing for water
Water statistics are never published

subtopics.title: Why Delivery Is Hard — Rural and Urban Challenges

questions.question: Serving dispersed rural settlements costs far more per household than serving a suburb because:
options: Rural households use more water
Small clusters of homes scattered across huge, often mountainous areas need long pipes for few users
Rural water must be imported
Suburbs receive no government funding

questions.question: When rural schemes break down, the burden falls heavily on women and children, who:
options: Repair the pumps themselves
Move permanently to the cities
Walk kilometres carrying water containers, at a cost in school hours, safety and health
Are always supplied first by tankers

questions.question: Non-revenue water is:
options: Water exported to neighbouring countries
Rainwater collected in tanks
The free basic allowance
Treated water lost to leaks, faulty meters or use that is never billed — a third or more of municipal water nationally

questions.question: Informal settlements are especially hard to serve because they:
options: Grow faster than pipes can follow, often on unplanned land such as floodplains or steep ground
Refuse municipal connections
Are always far from any city
Use more water per household than suburbs

subtopics.title: Big Engineering — Transfers, Dams and Purification

questions.question: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project works by gravity because:
options: The Vaal flows uphill into Lesotho
Its pumps are powered by coal
The Lesotho highlands catch the region's heaviest precipitation AND stand higher than Gauteng, so tunnel water flows down to the Vaal system
Gauteng lies at sea level

questions.question: Lesotho's side of the bargain includes:
options: Free electricity from Gauteng
Royalties that rank among its largest revenue sources, plus hydro-electric power
Ownership of the Vaal Dam
A share of South Africa's gold mines

questions.question: The Tugela-Vaal scheme differs from the Lesotho scheme because it:
options: Moves water by canal boat
Carries water to Cape Town
Requires no infrastructure
Must pump water UP the escarpment into Sterkfontein Dam, fighting gravity at great cost

questions.question: The correct order of municipal water purification is:
options: Screening, coagulation and flocculation, sedimentation, filtration, disinfection
Disinfection, filtration, sedimentation, coagulation, screening
Filtration, screening, disinfection, sedimentation, coagulation
Sedimentation, screening, disinfection, coagulation, filtration

subtopics.title: Sustainable Water Use — Government and Individuals

questions.question: Sustainable water use means:
options: Using as much water as the dams currently hold
Meeting today's needs without crippling tomorrow's supply — using no faster than the system replenishes
Banning all irrigation
Importing water from wetter countries

questions.question: Working for Water is celebrated as a double win because it:
options: Builds dams and sells electricity
Exports water and earns royalties
Employs thousands to clear thirsty alien plants, returning runoff to rivers while creating jobs
Drills boreholes and sells pumps

questions.question: Greywater, which individuals can reuse on gardens, is:
options: Water from the toilet
Borehole water
Rainwater from the roof
Gently used water from basins, baths and washing machines

questions.question: During the 2018 Day Zero crisis, Cape Town's consumption:
options: Was roughly halved — from about a thousand million litres a day toward five hundred million — through saving measures
Doubled as people stockpiled
Stayed exactly the same
Fell only because rain returned immediately

questions.question: Twenty-five litres per person per day is best understood as:
options: The average suburban consumption
A floor covering drinking, cooking and a basic wash — a single shower can use more
Enough for a garden and a pool
The amount lost to leaks per person

questions.question: The swimming pool subsidises the standpipe describes:
options: A rule that pools must be shared
Free water for sports facilities
Municipal pools heated by boreholes
Heavy users in expensive tariff blocks funding the free basic blocks of poor households

questions.question: The constitutional anchor of the free basic water policy is:
options: Section 27 — everyone's right of access to sufficient water
The municipal by-law on pipes
The Blue Drop certificate
The rising block tariff schedule

subtopics.title: Moving a River Over a Mountain

questions.question: The two facts that make the Lesotho Highlands scheme work are:
options: Lesotho has more people and more pumps
Lesotho catches the region's heaviest rain and snow, and stands far higher than Johannesburg
Lesotho has desalination plants and a coastline
Lesotho shares the Vaal Dam and the Orange mouth

questions.question: The dams built high in the Maluti mountains for the scheme include:
options: Gariep and Vanderkloof
Vaal Dam and Sterkfontein
Katse and Mohale, with Polihali being added
Theewaterskloof and Berg River

questions.question: Gravity is free; fighting gravity is expensive contrasts:
options: Dams against boreholes
Screening against filtration
Rural against urban supply
The Lesotho tunnels flowing downhill against Tugela-Vaal pumping up the escarpment

questions.question: In the kitchen version of purification, stir in a pinch that makes the fine dirt clump stands for:
options: Coagulation and flocculation with a chemical such as aluminium sulphate
Screening with metal grids
Chlorine disinfection
Sand filtration

subtopics.title: The City That Counted Its Days

questions.question: Day Zero was:
options: The day Cape Town's dams overflowed
The published date on which Cape Town's municipal taps would be turned off, with residents queuing for a 25-litre daily ration
A national holiday celebrating rain
The start of the Lesotho Highlands project

questions.question: The most important lesson of the Cape Town crisis is that:
options: Only new dams can save a city
Droughts never last three years
The cheapest, fastest new supply is the water people stop wasting — the city halved its use through millions of small decisions
Desalination alone kept the taps open

questions.question: Neither half works alone means:
options: Saving citizens with rotten pipes still lose the water, and perfect pipes with careless households still drain the dams
Rural and urban areas must share dams
The two Lesotho dams must operate together
Screening fails without disinfection

questions.question: Which belongs on the INDIVIDUAL's half of the sustainability list?
options: Auditing municipal water quality through Blue Drop
Building the Polihali Dam
Enforcing the National Water Act against polluters
Harvesting roof rainwater, reusing greywater and watering the garden in the cool of evening
